### A classical assessment {#projects-exam}

The course mixes theory and labs, so this proposal follows the balanced default of the master for units without a published mode: a written exam on the proved results, two short lab notebooks and one project. The weights are ours.

| Component | Weight | Format | Covers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Written exam | 50 % | 2 h, closed book, one handwritten A4 sheet | ch. 0–9 (the in-class chapters) |
| Lab notebooks | 20 % | two notebooks, 10 % each: tokenizer cost study and mini-GPT; a RAG pipeline with RAGAS evaluation | sessions 1–3 and 6–7 |
| Project | 30 % | one card of the [list below](#projects-list), at most 20 h per student, report and 10-minute oral | the chapters of the card |

**Resit.** A 2 h written exam in the same format replaces the exam mark; the notebook and project marks are kept, and a failed project may be resubmitted once.

**Sample questions.** Six questions worth 20 points in total, for the full 2 h paper.

**Q1 (4 pts) — KV-cache arithmetic.** A decoder has 40 layers, 32 query heads, 8 KV heads and $d_{\text{head}}=128$, with the cache in fp16. (a) Compute the cache size per token. (b) Compute the cache for a batch of 16 sequences of 8,192 tokens. (c) Same question with full multi-head attention (32 KV heads). (d) In one sentence, why is decoding limited by memory bandwidth rather than by FLOPs?

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- Formula of Prop. 2.4 with the factor 2 for K and V (1 pt).
- $2\times40\times8\times128\times2=163{,}840$ bytes $=160$ KiB per token (1 pt).
- $16\times8{,}192=131{,}072$ tokens, so 20 GiB with GQA and 80 GiB with full attention, a factor 4 (1 pt).
- Each new token reads all the weights and the whole cache for very few operations per byte (1 pt). Common error: multiplying by the 32 query heads instead of the 8 KV heads.
:::

**Q2 (4 pts) — From the KL-penalised objective to DPO.** For a fixed prompt $x$, show that the maximiser of
$$\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi}\big[r(x,y)\big]-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}\big(\pi\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\big)$$
is $\pi^\star\propto\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\,e^{r/\beta}$. Deduce the DPO loss from the Bradley–Terry model, and explain why the partition function disappears.

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- Rewrite the objective as
  $$-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}\big(\pi\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}e^{r/\beta}/Z\big)+\beta\log Z(x)$$
  (1.5 pts).
- The KL vanishes at $\pi^\star=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}e^{r/\beta}/Z(x)$ (0.5 pt).
- Invert:
  $$r(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi^\star(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)}+\beta\log Z(x)$$
  (1 pt).
- In $\sigma(r^+-r^-)$ the term $\beta\log Z(x)$ is the same for both responses and cancels, which gives Thm 5.2 with $\pi_\theta$ in place of $\pi^\star$ (1 pt). Common error: letting $Z$ depend on $y$.
:::

**Q3 (3 pts) — The Chinchilla optimum.** Using $C=6ND$ and $D^\star\approx20N^\star$ (Thm 3.1), compute $N^\star$ and $D^\star$ for $C=5.76\times10^{23}$ FLOP. Llama-3-8B was trained on 15T tokens: compute its compute budget and its tokens per parameter, and explain why it is far from the optimum on purpose.

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- $C=6N\cdot20N=120N^2$, so $N^\star=\sqrt{C/120}\approx6.9\times10^{10}$ (69B) and $D^\star\approx1.4\times10^{12}$ tokens, the Chinchilla model itself (1 pt).
- Llama-3-8B:
  $$C=6\times8\times10^{9}\times15\times10^{12}=7.2\times10^{23}\ \text{FLOP},$$
  and 1,875 tokens per parameter; the Chinchilla optimum for that budget is about 77B (1 pt).
- The law minimises training loss at a fixed training budget; a small, over-trained model is cheaper at inference, which dominates the total cost (1 pt). Common error: calling Llama-3-8B "undertrained".
:::

**Q4 (3 pts) — Speculative decoding.** (a) Show that one step of Thm 6.3 outputs a token distributed according to $p$. (b) With acceptance rate $\alpha=0.75$, $\gamma=3$ draft tokens and a draft step costing $c=0.1$ target forward, compute the expected number of tokens per target forward and the speed-up.

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- Acceptance contributes $\min(q,p)$ and the resampled residual $\max(0,p-q)$; their sum is $p$ (1.5 pts).
- Expected tokens per round (Ex. 10):
  $$\frac{1-\alpha^{\gamma+1}}{1-\alpha}=\frac{1-0.75^{4}}{0.25}\approx2.73$$
  (1 pt).
- Speed-up $2.73/(1+\gamma c)=2.73/1.3\approx2.1$ (0.5 pt). Common error: $1/(1-\alpha)=4$, which ignores the truncation at $\gamma$.
:::

**Q5 (3 pts) — Watermark test.** A detector with green fraction $\gamma=0.25$ reads $T=200$ tokens and counts 70 green ones. Compute $z$ (Thm 9.3) and decide at the one-sided 1 % level. A user keeps only the first 50 tokens, with the same green fraction: what happens?

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- The z-score:
  $$z=\frac{70-50}{\sqrt{200\times0.25\times0.75}}=\frac{20}{6.12}\approx3.27$$
  (1 pt).
- One-sided p-value $\approx5\times10^{-4}<0.01$: reject "human text" (1 pt).
- With the same green fraction, $z$ scales like $\sqrt{T}$: $3.27\times\sqrt{50/200}\approx1.63$, below even the 5 % threshold 1.645, so the mark is no longer detected (1 pt). Common error: using $\gamma=1/2$ in the variance.
:::

**Q6 (3 pts) — Is model A better than model B?** Both models answer the same 1,000 questions: A is right on 812, B on 790; A is right and B wrong on 62 items, the reverse on 40. A colleague runs an unpaired two-proportion test and finds $p\approx0.22$. Run the right test and conclude.

::: proof
[Marking points]{.tag}

- The design is paired, so McNemar's test applies (9.1) (1 pt).
- $\chi^2=(62-40)^2/(62+40)=484/102\approx4.75$, $p\approx0.03$ with one degree of freedom (exact binomial test: 0.037): significant at 5 % (1 pt).
- The unpaired test treats the 750 items both models get right and the 148 both get wrong as noise; only the 102 discordant items carry information (1 pt). Common error: concluding "no difference" from the unpaired test.
:::

### Projects {#projects-list}

House rules: public data, a laptop CPU or one free Colab T4, open models only (inference up to 8B in 4-bit, training up to 1.5B with LoRA), and only what this module and its prerequisites teach. Levels ★/★★/★★★ are those of the exercises; for this 24 h, 2 ECTS course a card asks at most 20 h per student.

**Grading grid used by every project of this page** (a project card may replace one row).

| Criterion | Weight |
|---|---|
| Question and success metric stated before the experiments | 10 % |
| Correct use of the course results (cited by number) | 25 % |
| Protocol: leakage-free split, baselines, at least 3 seeds, intervals | 25 % |
| Results and analysis: error analysis, limits, one responsible-AI remark | 20 % |
| Reproducibility: repository, README, pinned environment, one command | 10 % |
| Communication: report (≤ 6 pages solo, ≤ 10 group) or 10-minute oral | 10 % |

Group projects: a contribution statement and an oral with individual questions; the individual grade is the group grade times a factor in [0.8, 1.2].

Six Year-2 capstones of the transverse project build on this module: [C1](../m2-projet-transverse/index.html#c1) (medical-information assistant: hybrid RAG, citations and abstention, ch. 7 and 9), [C3](../m2-projet-transverse/index.html#c3) and [C5](../m2-projet-transverse/index.html#c5) (plain-language requests turned into structured specifications, ch. 8), [C4](../m2-projet-transverse/index.html#c4) (voice assistant over reviews, ch. 7–8), [C7](../m2-projet-transverse/index.html#c7) (internal assistant that must not leak personal data: GraphRAG, memorisation and the AI Act, ch. 7 and 9.6) and [C8](../m2-projet-transverse/index.html#c8) (public-agency assistant citing official pages, ch. 7 and 9).
